d: A severe, whole-body allergic reaction: airway swelling, wheezing, hives and falling blood pressure. Life-threatening; epinephrine is the first drug.
A contrast reaction that looks like allergy (hives, swelling, wheezing, anaphylaxis) even though most aren't true IgE allergy, so a first exposure can react.
A contrast reaction caused by the drug's direct effect on the body (nausea, flushing, vasovagal, arrhythmia, seizure), not by allergy. Needs no premedication later.
A nerve reflex that slows the heart and drops blood pressure: pale, sweaty, lightheaded, SLOW pulse, may faint. Treated with legs up, fluids, atropine if it persists.
A true allergy driven by IgE antibodies, which requires an earlier exposure to become sensitized.
Drugs (usually a steroid like prednisone, sometimes an antihistamine) given before contrast to lower the risk of a repeat allergic-like reaction.
Adrenaline. The first drug for anaphylaxis: opens the airways and raises blood pressure. IM dose for adults is 0.3 mg of the 1 mg/mL product.
An antihistamine for hives and itching. Sedating (no driving after). It does not treat anaphylaxis and never replaces epinephrine.
A drug that blocks histamine to ease hives and itching (e.g., diphenhydramine, promethazine).
Reversal agent for benzodiazepines like midazolam. Can wear off before the sedative and can cause seizures.
Reversal agent for opioids like morphine and fentanyl.
A class of sedative and anti-anxiety drugs: midazolam (Versed), diazepam, lorazepam. Reversed by flumazenil.
A class of strong pain relievers (morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone) that can slow breathing. Reversed by naloxone.
A short-acting benzodiazepine sedative used for procedures. Reversed by flumazenil. DEA Schedule IV.
A potent opioid, given IV or as a skin patch (Duragesic). Heat over a patch increases the dose absorbed.
An IV anesthetic used for sedation (looks like milk). It has no reversal agent; watch for apnea and low blood pressure.
An anticholinergic drug that speeds up a slow heart rate (e.g., a vasovagal reaction that doesn't settle).
An oral anticoagulant (blood thinner) that blocks vitamin K. Monitored with the INR; reversed with vitamin K1.
An anticoagulant. In imaging you mostly see it in flushes that keep catheters from clotting.
A drug that slows blood clotting (warfarin, heparin, apixaban). Patients bleed longer at puncture sites.
A drug that stops platelets from clumping (aspirin, clopidogrel), so puncture sites bleed longer.
A diabetes pill cleared unchanged by the kidneys. If kidney function suddenly drops it can build up and cause lactic acidosis.
A dangerous buildup of lactic acid in the blood. The worry with metformin when the kidneys fail.
A blood pressure and heart drug (e.g., metoprolol). Can blunt the effect of epinephrine during a reaction.
An anti-inflammatory drug. Used for contrast premedication; it raises blood glucose.
A rescue inhaler that relaxes the airway muscles in bronchospasm (asthma, wheezing).
Sudden tightening of the muscles around the airways, causing wheezing and shortness of breath.
Vitamin K1, the drug that reverses warfarin.
A hormone given by injection to raise blood glucose when a hypoglycemic patient can't safely take anything by mouth.
What the body does to a drug: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism (mostly liver), Excretion (mostly kidneys).
The liver breaks down part of a swallowed drug before it reaches the body, so oral doses are often bigger than IV doses.
The fraction of a dose that reaches the bloodstream unchanged. IV is 100%.
The time it takes for the drug level in the blood to fall by half.
The volume of plasma cleared of a drug per unit of time (mL/min).
How much drug it takes to get an effect. A drug that works at a low dose is potent.
The maximum effect a drug can produce, at any dose (the ceiling).
Under the tongue until it dissolves. Skips the first-pass effect.
Held against the cheek until it dissolves.
Injected into the skin layer itself, just under the surface (e.g., a TB skin test).
Injected into the fat under the skin; absorbs slowly. Write SUBQ, never SC or SQ.
Injected into a muscle (e.g., the outer thigh for epinephrine). Faster than subcutaneous.
Injected into the spinal fluid (subarachnoid space), as in myelography. Only agents labeled for this route.
A needle into the bone marrow (humerus, tibia, femur, sternum) for emergency access when an IV fails.
Any route that bypasses the GI tract, mainly injections (IV, IM, SUBQ).
Delivered through the skin from a patch (fentanyl, nitroglycerin, nicotine, scopolamine).
A tablet coating that keeps it from dissolving in the stomach. Never crush it.
A drug with abuse potential, regulated by the DEA in Schedules I–V. Kept locked and logged; waste is witnessed.
The DEA's legal classes for controlled drugs. I: high abuse, no medical use. II: high abuse, medical use (opioids). III: moderate. IV: lower (benzodiazepines). V: lowest.
Right patient, drug, dose, route, time, and documentation.
Collecting everything a patient takes, comparing it to what's ordered now, resolving problems, and passing the list on.
How concentrated a solution's particles are. Higher-osmolality contrast causes more heat, discomfort, fluid shift and physiologic reactions. Plasma is about 290 mOsm/kg.
Contrast with about the same osmolality as blood plasma (iodixanol/Visipaque, a nonionic dimer).
Contrast about 1–3 times plasma osmolality; most nonionic monomers (iohexol, iopamidol). The usual IV contrast.
Contrast with much higher osmolality than plasma (about 5x), e.g. diatrizoate. Draws water in; no longer given into vessels.
Contrast that splits into charged particles in solution, which raises osmolality.
Contrast that doesn't split into charged particles, so it has lower osmolality. Most modern IV contrast.
X-ray and CT contrast containing iodine. Excreted unchanged by the kidneys.
The metal in MRI contrast. It shortens T1 so enhancing tissue looks bright. Always bound in a chelate because free gadolinium is toxic.
A molecule that wraps around and holds gadolinium so the toxic free metal isn't released.
A ring-shaped gadolinium chelate that holds the metal tightly, with less retention in the body than linear agents.
A rare, serious thickening of the skin and organs after some gadolinium agents (mostly ACR Group I) in severe kidney disease or AKI.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate: how well the kidneys filter, calculated from serum creatinine. Lower means worse kidney function.
A muscle waste product cleared by the kidneys. Serum creatinine is used to calculate eGFR.
Blood urea nitrogen, a protein waste product cleared by the kidneys. It does not decide contrast kidney risk; eGFR does.
A sudden drop in kidney function over hours to days.
Positive GI contrast (bright white). A suspension, not a solution. Never used when perforation is suspected.
Solid particles mixed through a liquid without dissolving. They settle, so mix before use (barium).
A hole through the wall of the bowel or another hollow organ.
Inflammation of the lining of the abdominal cavity, e.g. from barium leaking through a perforation.
A hyperosmolar, water-soluble iodinated contrast for oral or bladder use. Draws water into the bowel and is harmful if aspirated.
Iodinated contrast that dissolves in water and is absorbed if it leaks, used instead of barium when a leak or perforation is possible.
Barium coats the lining while gas (air or CO2) distends the lumen, so small lesions stand out.
Absorbs x-rays and shows white (barium, iodine).
Lets x-rays through and shows dark (air, carbon dioxide).
How thick a fluid is. Thick contrast flows poorly through small catheters; warming it lowers viscosity.
INS: a VESICANT fluid or drug leaking into tissue, which can blister and kill tissue. In radiology the ACR calls any contrast leak extravasation.
INS: a NON-vesicant fluid or drug leaking out of the vein into surrounding tissue.
A drug or fluid that can cause blisters and tissue death if it leaks out of the vein.
An inflamed vein: red, warm, tender, sometimes a firm cord above the IV. Warm compress.
Air entering the bloodstream and blocking flow. Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, low BP. 100% oxygen and left side down.
Something traveling in the blood (clot, air, fat) that lodges and blocks a vessel.
A clot (usually from the legs) blocking an artery in the lungs: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, fast heart rate.
Pressure building inside a closed muscle compartment (e.g., the hand or forearm) that cuts off blood flow. A surgical emergency.
How fast color returns to a nail bed after you press it. Slow refill means poor blood flow.
Needle or catheter size. A HIGHER number means a SMALLER lumen (24 G small, 18 G large).
Catheter and tube size. Opposite of gauge: a higher number means BIGGER (1 Fr = 1/3 mm outside diameter).
The hollow channel inside a needle, catheter, tube or vessel.
The slanted tip of a needle. Inserted bevel up.
Blood appearing in the catheter's chamber, showing the needle tip is in the vein.
The inside bend of the elbow, where the median cubital, cephalic and basilic veins are; preferred for power injection.
The palm side of the hand or wrist. The volar wrist is avoided for IVs (painful, nerve injury risk).
The preferred skin antiseptic (in alcohol) before an IV. Scrub and let it dry completely.
A machine that injects contrast at a set rate and volume under pressure, for CT and MR timing. Only devices labeled for it.
A dose given all at once (by hand push or power injector) rather than dripped in slowly.
A flexible plastic IV catheter threaded over a needle; the needle comes out and the plastic stays in the vein.
A short steel needle with plastic wings for brief access or blood draws. It stays in the vein, so it dislodges easily; avoid for power injection.
A sealed glass single-dose container you snap open. Draw up through a filter needle, then change needles.
A container with a rubber stopper. Single-dose: one patient, once. Multiple-dose: has a preservative, discard 28 days after opening.
Peripherally inserted central catheter: put in through an upper-arm vein with the tip near the heart (lower SVC).
A catheter whose tip sits in a large central vein near the heart (SVC/cavoatrial junction). PICCs and ports count.
A small reservoir under the chest skin connected to a central-vein catheter, reached through the skin with a non-coring (Huber) needle.
A specially angled needle used to access an implanted port without cutting a core out of its rubber septum.
A central line run under the skin from the vein to a chest exit site, for long-term chemo or TPN.
A valve at the tip of some tunneled catheters and PICCs, not its own type of line.
Where the superior vena cava meets the right atrium; where an upper-body central line tip should sit.
The large vein that returns blood from the upper body into the right atrium.
Total parenteral nutrition: concentrated IV feeding, given through a central line because it would injure a small vein.
The ridge where the trachea splits into the right and left main bronchi. ETT tip sits about 5 cm above it.
A breathing tube passed through the mouth or nose into the trachea, sealed by an inflated cuff.
An opening in the front of the neck into the trachea, with a tube held by neck ties.
The guide used to insert a tracheostomy tube. It travels with a patient who has a new trach.
Having a window. A fenestrated trach tube has an opening above the cuff so air reaches the vocal cords.
A machine that breathes for the patient through a tube. Never unplug it or open the circuit.
Negative pressure that pulls secretions or stomach contents out. Only qualified staff suction an airway.
A tube from the nose into the stomach to drain it, or to give feeds, drugs or contrast.
Like an NG tube, but placed through the mouth.
A tube from the nose past the stomach into the duodenum or jejunum. The technologist never removes it.
A small-bore feeding tube with a weighted tip, placed over a wire stylet.
A double-lumen NG tube for drainage under suction, with a blue air vent (pigtail) that is never clamped.
A single-lumen gastric tube with holes near the tip, for decompression, drainage and lavage.
A feeding tube through the abdominal wall directly into the stomach.
Where the esophagus joins the stomach. An NG tip must be well past it.
The first part of the small intestine, right after the stomach.
The middle section of the small intestine.
A tube with gastric and esophageal balloons that press on bleeding esophageal varices. ICU only.
Swollen veins in the esophagus (often from liver disease) that can bleed heavily.
Stopping bleeding by pressing on it, e.g. with an inflated balloon.
Draining air or fluid to relieve pressure, e.g. emptying the stomach with an NG tube.
Washing out a body cavity (e.g., the stomach) with fluid.
Breathing fluid, food or vomit into the airway and lungs. (Also: drawing fluid back with a syringe.)
Air in the pleural space, collapsing part of the lung.
Air that enters the pleural space and can't escape, building pressure on the heart and lungs. An emergency.
Blood in the pleural space.
Fluid (other than blood) collecting in the pleural space.
The thin space between the lung and the chest wall.
The chamber of a chest drain with a shallow column of water acting as a one-way valve: air leaves the chest but can't return.
The water in a chest drain's water seal rising and falling with breathing, showing the tube is open to the pleural space.
A balloon-tipped catheter floated through the right heart into the pulmonary artery to measure heart pressures and output.
Death of lung tissue from blocked blood flow.
A device that paces a heart that beats too slowly or has a conduction block.
An implanted device that shocks dangerous fast ventricular rhythms (and transvenous ones can also pace).
The electrical firing of heart muscle cells that triggers them to contract.
Heart muscle cells electrically resetting after firing, ready for the next beat.
The first small bump on the ECG: the atria depolarize.
The tall spike on the ECG: the ventricles depolarize. (Atrial repolarization is hidden inside it.)
The bump after the QRS on the ECG: the ventricles repolarize.
Electrocardiogram: a tracing of the heart's electrical activity.
Irregularly irregular rhythm with no distinct P waves; the atria quiver instead of beating. Makes cardiac gating hard.
An early, wide, bizarre beat with no P wave, followed by a pause.
Chaotic quivering of the ventricles with no pulse. Shockable: CPR and defibrillation.
A very fast rhythm from the ventricles. Without a pulse it's shockable.
No electrical activity at all. Not shockable: CPR.
An organized rhythm on the monitor but no pulse in the patient. Not shockable: treat as cardiac arrest with CPR.
Heart rate above 100 beats per minute in an adult.
Heart rate below 60 beats per minute in an adult.
Breathing faster than normal.
Difficult or labored breathing; shortness of breath.
No breathing.
Not enough oxygen reaching the tissues.
A bluish color of skin or lips from low oxygen.
A high-pitched noise on breathing in, from a narrowed upper airway (e.g., laryngeal swelling). An emergency sign.
A whistling sound from narrowed lower airways (asthma, bronchospasm).
Swelling of the voice box that can block the airway; hoarseness can be an early sign.
Low blood pressure.
High blood pressure.
A drop of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing. Causes dizziness and falls.
Fainting: a brief loss of consciousness from too little blood flow to the brain.
Shock from too little blood volume (bleeding, dehydration): fast pulse, cool clammy skin.
Shock because the heart pump is failing.
Shock after a spinal cord injury: vessels dilate, so low BP with a SLOW pulse and warm, dry skin.
Shock from blood vessels dilating too much (anaphylactic, septic, neurogenic).
Shock where the heart works but something blocks the circuit (e.g., a large PE or tension pneumothorax).
Low blood glucose: shaky, sweaty, pale, confused, within minutes. Classic setup: fasted for the study but took usual insulin.
High blood glucose: warm dry skin, thirst, drowsy, develops over hours to days.
A high-glucose emergency (more often type 1) with deep rapid breathing and fruity breath.
Stroke symptoms that fully resolve. A warning that a larger stroke may follow; worked up urgently.
Ischemia = too little blood flow. An ischemic stroke is a blocked brain artery (about 7 in 8 strokes).
A stroke from a ruptured vessel bleeding into or around the brain.
The last time the patient was seen at their normal neurologic baseline. The stroke treatment clock starts here.
A language problem: trouble finding or understanding words. The brain's language centers are affected, not the mouth.
Slurred or effortful speech from weak or uncoordinated speech muscles; language itself is intact.
Trouble sequencing the movements of speech, so sounds come out in the wrong order.
Automated external defibrillator: analyzes the rhythm and tells you when to shock.
An electric shock to the heart to stop VF or pulseless VT so a normal rhythm can restart.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions (plus breaths) for a patient with no pulse.
Breaths given to someone who has a pulse but isn't breathing normally: adults 1 every 6 s, children and infants 1 every 2–3 s.
A team called for a patient who is getting worse but hasn't arrested (a code is for arrest).
The usual call for cardiac or respiratory arrest. Give code type, age group and exact location.
Uncontrolled electrical activity in the brain, often with jerking movements and loss of awareness.
An indwelling urinary catheter held in the bladder by a balloon filled with sterile water.
Above the pubic bone. A suprapubic catheter goes through the lower abdominal wall into the bladder.
A tube through the skin into the kidney to drain urine.
A drain placed in the common bile duct after gallbladder or bile duct surgery.
An opening of bowel (or another organ) brought out onto the skin of the abdomen.
A surgically created opening (stoma), named for where it opens (ileostomy, colostomy).
A stoma from the ileum (small bowel); output is liquid to paste-like.
A stoma from the colon; output gets firmer the farther along the colon it is.
A surgical drain with a squeezed bulb that creates suction. Don't let the bulb hang by its tubing.
A spring-loaded surgical drain that creates suction, often after joint surgery.
A soft open drain that works by gravity, with a safety pin so it can't slip into the wound.
Flowing backward against the normal direction, e.g. contrast up a bladder catheter or by enema.
Flowing forward in the normal direction, e.g. contrast down an NG tube.
Contrast injected up the ureter through a cystoscope to show the ureter and collecting system (not kidney function).
For germs that float in the air over distance (TB, measles, chickenpox): negative-pressure room and a fit-tested N95.
For germs spread by large droplets within about 3–6 feet (influenza, pertussis, mumps): a surgical mask on entering.
For germs spread by touch (C. diff, MRSA, VRE): gown and gloves.
A fit-tested respirator that filters airborne particles. Used for airborne precautions.
A room where air flows in but not out to the hallway, keeping airborne germs contained.
Personal protective equipment: gloves, gowns, masks, respirators, eye protection.
Taking off PPE. Gloves come off before you touch your face, the gown is peeled so the outside ends up inside, hand hygiene last.
Putting on PPE.
A gut bacterium whose spores alcohol hand rub can't kill: wash with soap and water. Contact precautions.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus: a staph bacterium resistant to many antibiotics.
Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus: a gut bacterium resistant to vancomycin.
Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers: bacteria that destroy many common antibiotics.
A highly contagious stomach virus. Alcohol hand rub doesn't work well against it: soap and water.
Too few infection-fighting white cells (or a weakened immune system), so the patient needs protective (reverse) isolation.
Precautions that protect a patient with weak immunity from staff and visitors' germs.
Sorts items by infection risk: critical (enters sterile tissue → sterilize), semicritical (touches mucous membranes → high-level disinfection), noncritical (intact skin → clean/low-level).
Killing ALL microorganisms, including spores (e.g., steam autoclave).
Killing most microorganisms, but not necessarily all spores.
A machine that sterilizes with pressurized steam; preferred for heat-tolerant items.
The area kept free of all microorganisms during a procedure. Only sterile items and gloved hands touch it.
The links an infection needs: agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, susceptible host. Break any link to stop it.
The federal law protecting patients' health information. Looking at a record you don't need for your job is a violation.
Legal permission from a STATE to practice there.
Keeping your ARRT credential active: annual renewal, CE requirements and ethics attestation.
Earning the ARRT credential by meeting education and ethics requirements and passing the exam.
American Registry of Radiologic Technologists: certifies and registers technologists, sets ethics rules and CE requirements.
American Society of Radiologic Technologists: the professional society you join as a member; publishes the Practice Standards and scope of practice.
Joint Review Committee on Education in Radiologic Technology: accredits educational programs.
Required ongoing education to keep ARRT registration (24 credits every 2 years).
What a technologist is educated, competent and legally allowed to do. State law and facility policy can narrow it.
A patient's agreement after a conversation about purpose, method, risks, benefits and alternatives. Obtained by the licensed practitioner; can be withdrawn.
Do not resuscitate: no CPR if the heart or breathing stops. Other care, including for a patient who is struggling but has a pulse, continues.
A legal document stating a patient's wishes for care if they can't speak for themselves.

t: durable power of attorney for health care
d: An advance directive naming someone the patient trusts to make health decisions when the patient can't.
Communication that helps the patient express feelings and feel heard (reflecting, restating, open-ended questions), not reassuring or changing the subject.
How something is said, not the words: tone, pitch, rate, volume, pauses.
Body language: gestures, posture, facial expression, eye movement.
Asking the patient to explain or show the instructions back to you, to confirm they understood.
A question that can't be answered yes or no, inviting the patient to explain.
A battery device held against the neck that lets a patient who lost their voice box speak.
Skin and tissue damage from prolonged pressure, usually over bone. Staged 1–4, plus unstageable and deep tissue.
Tissue layers sliding against each other (e.g., dragging a patient), tearing deeper tissue.
Places where bone is close to the skin (sacrum, heels, scapulae, elbows): highest pressure injury risk.
A belt around the patient's waist that you hold to support them during standing and transfers.
Sitting up in bed. High Fowler: upright (~90°); semi-Fowler: head raised about 30–45°.
Lying flat with the head lower than the feet.
Anything that restricts a patient's movement beyond ordinary transport safety. Needs an order and follows restraint policy; not a fall-prevention device.
The 16-section sheet that comes with every hazardous chemical. Section 4 is first aid.
Fire response: Rescue, Alarm, Contain/Confine, Extinguish/Evacuate.
Using an extinguisher: Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep.
A clip that estimates oxygen saturation of the blood. Cold hands, shivering, nail polish and a BP cuff on the same arm can give false readings.
The heartbeat heard with a stethoscope over the apex of the heart. Used for infants and when the radial pulse is irregular or weak.
The pulse in the neck. Check one side at a time with light pressure.
The top blood pressure number: pressure when the heart contracts.
The bottom blood pressure number: pressure when the heart relaxes between beats.
International normalized ratio: a standardized clotting test. About 0.8–1.2 without anticoagulants; higher means slower clotting.
A blood clotting test (seconds), reported along with the INR.
Activated partial thromboplastin time: a clotting test in seconds, used to monitor heparin.
Human chorionic gonadotropin: the pregnancy hormone measured in pregnancy tests.
An oxygen mask that delivers a set, precise oxygen concentration regardless of how the patient breathes.
An oxygen mask with a reservoir bag and one-way valves so exhaled air can't enter the bag; delivers high concentrations.
Oxygen tubing with two prongs in the nostrils; low-flow.
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry: a low-dose scan of bone mineral density, usually lumbar spine and hip.
DXA result compared with a healthy young adult. −1.0 or above normal; −1.0 to −2.5 osteopenia; −2.5 or below osteoporosis.
DXA result compared with people of the same age and sex.
Low bone density with fragile bones and high fracture risk (T-score −2.5 or below).
Bone density lower than normal but not yet osteoporosis (T-score between −1.0 and −2.5).
3D mammography: the tube sweeps in an arc over the compressed breast and builds thin slices.
Mammography Quality Standards Act: federal rules for mammography, including sending results letters on time.
Craniocaudal: the top-to-bottom mammography view.
Mediolateral oblique: the angled side mammography view.
The depth where protons dump most of their energy, with almost no exit dose beyond it. Why proton therapy spares tissue.
Radiation therapy with protons, which stop at a set depth (Bragg peak). Used for children and tumors near critical structures.
The machine that produces high-energy x-rays for external beam radiation therapy.
Radiation therapy aimed at the body from a machine outside it. The patient doesn't become radioactive.
A radioactive drug given for nuclear medicine imaging; a gamma camera images where it goes.
Positron emission tomography: shows function (e.g., glucose use). Combined with CT or MRI to show where that activity is in the anatomy.
Fluorodeoxyglucose: a radioactive glucose analog taken up by active tissue, including many cancers. The usual PET tracer.
Single-photon emission CT: 3D nuclear medicine imaging with a gamma camera.
A nuclear medicine scan of liver bile flow; looks for cholecystitis and bile leaks.
Ventilation/perfusion lung scan (inhaled + IV tracer) to look for pulmonary embolism.
An area of INCREASED tracer uptake on a nuclear medicine image. (Cold spot = decreased.)
Inflammation of the gallbladder.
Cancer that has spread from where it started to other parts of the body.
Contrast injected into the subarachnoid space (usually by lumbar puncture), then x-rays and CT of the spinal canal.
The space around the spinal cord and brain that holds cerebrospinal fluid.
A needle into the spinal canal in the lower back to sample fluid or inject contrast.
Contrast injected into a joint, then imaged.
Vascular access method: needle into the vessel, guidewire through the needle, needle out, catheter over the wire.
A thin flexible wire used to guide a catheter into a vessel.
Opening a narrowed artery with a balloon, usually followed by a stent.
An artery narrowing again after angioplasty or stenting.
Deliberately blocking a blood vessel through a catheter (e.g., to stop bleeding or feed to a tumor).
U.S. Preventive Services Task Force: an expert panel that issues screening recommendations.
American College of Radiology: publishes the Manual on Contrast Media, MR safety guidance and accreditation standards.
Infusion Nurses Society: sets IV practice standards (e.g., the infiltration vs extravasation definitions, 2-attempt limit).
Institute for Safe Medication Practices: publishes the list of error-prone abbreviations and dose designations.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: federal infection control guidance.
Food and Drug Administration: approves drugs and devices, regulates labeling.
Drug Enforcement Administration: regulates controlled substances and their schedules.
Pro re nata: as needed.
Immediately.
Nil per os: nothing by mouth.
Medication administration record: where every drug given is charted, right after it's given.
A zero after the decimal point (5.0 mg). Never write it: it can be misread as 50.
A zero before the decimal point (0.5 mg). Always write it: .5 can be misread as 5.
An order spoken rather than written. Write it down, read it back, get confirmation.
The facility's internal report of an error or near miss. Never mentioned in or filed with the patient's chart.
An item with no known hazards in any MR environment (ASTM green square icon).
Safe only under specific conditions (field strength, SAR, etc.) listed in its labeling (yellow triangle icon).
Known to pose a hazard in all MR environments; never enters Zone III or IV (red icon).
American Society for Testing and Materials: wrote the MR Safe / Conditional / Unsafe labeling terms.
Strongly attracted to a magnet (iron, steel). Can become a projectile near the MRI.
A ferromagnetic object pulled into the magnet at high speed.
Rapid boil-off of the liquid helium that shuts down the superconducting magnet's field.
Specific absorption rate: RF energy deposited in the body (W/kg), the cause of heating.
Flashes of light seen when moving the head quickly in a strong magnetic field.
ACR MRI Zone III: restricted area next to the magnet room; only screened people, supervised by MR personnel.
ACR MRI Zone IV: the magnet room itself. The cart and defibrillator never enter it.
The main static magnetic field of the scanner. Always on, 24/7.
A magnetic field that changes across space, used for spatial encoding. Switching causes the noise and can stimulate nerves (PNS).
Radiofrequency: the energy pulses that excite protons; they can heat tissue (SAR).
Peripheral nerve stimulation: twitching or tingling from rapidly switching gradients.
The frequency protons precess at: field strength × gyromagnetic ratio (42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen). 63.9 MHz at 1.5 T.
The wobbling spin of a proton around the magnetic field direction.
Spin-lattice relaxation: recovery of longitudinal magnetization after the RF pulse.
Spin-spin relaxation: loss of transverse magnetization as protons dephase.
Repetition time: time between successive excitation pulses. Short TR → T1 weighting.
Echo time: time from excitation to the echo. Long TE → T2 weighting.
Inversion time: delay after an inversion pulse, chosen to null a tissue (fat in STIR, fluid in FLAIR).
Image contrast based on how many hydrogen protons a tissue has (long TR, short TE).
Signal-to-noise ratio: how much signal compared with background noise. Thinner slices or smaller voxels lower it.
Number of excitations (signal averages). Doubling NEX doubles scan time and raises SNR by about 41% (√2).
Field of view: the size of the area imaged.
A 3D pixel: the volume of tissue each image point represents.
Short tau inversion recovery: an inversion recovery sequence that nulls fat. Good for edema and marrow (e.g., osteomyelitis).
Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery: a long-TI inversion recovery that nulls fluid (CSF).
Gradient echo: a sequence with a flip angle under 90° and no 180° refocusing pulse; sensitive to blood products and metal (T2*).
Signal loss and distortion near metal or air, from local magnetic field differences.
Artifact at fat–water boundaries because fat and water precess at slightly different frequencies.
Thin parallel lines near sharp edges from too little sampling; can mimic a syrinx. Fix by increasing the matrix.
Anatomy outside the field of view folding into the image in the phase direction.
The image direction encoded by phase; motion artifact and aliasing show up along it.
The range of frequencies sampled. Wider bandwidth reduces metal and chemical shift artifact but lowers SNR.
A pulse that suppresses fat signal by its frequency. Fails near metal, so avoid it with hardware.
A band that nulls signal from tissue outside the area of interest (e.g., over the throat to cut swallowing artifact).
A fluid-filled cavity inside the spinal cord.
Infection of bone.
Cerebrospinal fluid: the clear fluid around the brain and spinal cord.
A therapeutic technique: sending the patient’s idea or feeling back to them so they explore it and reach their own decision.
A therapeutic technique: checking that you understood what the patient reported, e.g. “You’re saying the pain is worse when you lie flat?”
A therapeutic technique: saying out loud the feeling you notice, e.g. “You seem tense.”
A block to communication: “Don’t worry, everything will be fine.” It dismisses the patient’s feelings.
A question answered with yes, no or one word. Fine for facts, poor for feelings.
Moisture wicking organisms through a sterile wrapper. A damp or wet pack is unsterile.
Fever: a temperature of 100.4 °F (38.0 °C) or higher.
Body temperature below 95.0 °F (35.0 °C).
The area under you between your feet. Feet about shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, gives a stable base for lifting.
Moving and lifting safely: wide base, lift with the legs, keep the load close, turn with your feet instead of twisting.
An electrical fire (energized equipment). Use CO2 or ABC dry chemical, never water.
Two patient-specific details (usually full name and date of birth), checked against the wristband and the order. Never a room number.
A nosebleed. Pinch the soft part of the nose and lean forward; never tilt the head back.
The fluid surrounding the fetus in the uterus; it helps keep the fetus cool during MRI.
Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion: the four steps of pharmacokinetics.
A bacterial lung infection spread through the air. Airborne precautions: negative-pressure room and N95.
Memory aid for AIRBORNE precautions: Measles, TB, Varicella (chickenpox).
Inflammation/infection of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord. Bacterial (meningococcal) meningitis is droplet.
Sore, inflamed throat; streptococcal pharyngitis is a droplet-precaution infection.
The organization that accredits hospitals and sets safety standards (e.g., restraints, time-outs, drills).
The clinician who manages ventilators, oxygen therapy and airway suctioning.
Methylene diphosphonate: the technetium-99m tracer used for bone scans.
Filtering the blood by machine (or through the abdomen) when the kidneys have failed.
ARRT Continuing Qualification Requirements: a self-assessment every 10 years for credentials earned since 2011.
Shortness of breath.
International unit. An error-prone abbreviation (can be read as IV); write “units” or “international units.”
Error-prone abbreviations: MS/MSO4 (morphine sulfate) and MgSO4 (magnesium sulfate) get confused. Write the full drug name.
Per os: by mouth.
Last menstrual period: asked privately when screening for pregnancy.
A large neck vein, a common site for nontunneled central lines.
The space between two ribs (e.g., 4th ICS for the V1 ECG lead or a chest tube at the 4th–5th ICS).
Vitamin K3. Not the warfarin reversal agent (that’s vitamin K1, phytonadione).
Gadolinium agents with the most NSF cases (Omniscan, Magnevist, OptiMARK). Contraindicated with AKI or eGFR below 30.
Gadolinium agents with few, if any, unconfounded NSF cases. Kidney screening optional at standard doses.
Monitoring of exhaled carbon dioxide; shows breathing during sedation and confirms an ET tube is in the trachea.
Over the counter: sold without a prescription.
American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology; co-wrote the 2025 contrast premedication consensus with the ACR.
American Cancer Society: publishes its own cancer screening schedules.
Redness from increased blood flow. Blanchable redness over a pressure point is the first warning of a pressure injury.
Death of tissue.
Americans with Disabilities Act: requires effective communication (e.g., sign-language interpreters) for deaf patients.
How awake and responsive a patient is. A change is often the earliest sign of trouble.
A 3–15 score of eye, verbal and motor response used to track level of consciousness.
Pressure inside the skull. Rising ICP first shows as a change in level of consciousness.
Vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
The RF magnetic field transmitted to excite protons; the source of SAR heating.
Root-mean-square: an average of a varying signal, used for B1 exposure limits (B1+RMS).
The ASTM standard defining the MR Safe / Conditional / Unsafe labels and icons.
Image contrast driven by T1 (short TR, short TE): fat bright, fluid dark.
Image contrast driven by T2 (long TR, long TE): fluid bright.
Fast (turbo) spin echo: several echoes per TR to shorten scan time.
An iron-storage breakdown product of old blood; shows as dark blooming on GRE images.
A side-to-side curve of the spine; best shown in the coronal plane.
A forward (outward) rounding curve of the spine, normal in the thoracic region.
An inward curve of the spine, normal in the cervical and lumbar regions.
Date of birth; one of the two patient identifiers (with full name).
Continuous (CPAP) or bilevel (BiPAP) positive airway pressure: positive-pressure breathing support through a tight mask, with no tube in the airway.
Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support: the advanced resuscitation training (rhythms, drugs, defibrillation) beyond basic CPR.
The flat stretch of the ECG between the QRS and the T wave. Elevation or depression can signal heart ischemia (but is distorted inside an MRI).
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin). Risks: GI bleeding and kidney injury.
A pain and fever reliever that is not anti-inflammatory. Liver toxicity in overdose.
Acute kidney injury that FOLLOWS contrast, whatever the actual cause.
Acute kidney injury actually CAUSED by the contrast.
Radiology information system: the department software for orders, scheduling and exam records.
An advanced-practice nurse who can prescribe and order exams where state law allows.
A licensed clinician who can prescribe and order exams where state law allows.
A 2009 federal law that strengthened HIPAA privacy, security and enforcement.
HIPAA habit: share only the patient information the other person needs for the task, not the whole record.
A dry-chemical fire extinguisher rated for class A (ordinary), B (flammable liquid) and C (electrical) fires.
A medical product made by living cells, such as a vaccine or blood product. Regulated by FDA licensure.
When repeated doses keep a drug level stable; reached after about 4–5 half-lives.
Drug attached to blood proteins. It is inactive and held in reserve; only free (unbound) drug acts.
A local anesthetic that is also an antiarrhythmic drug.
An antiarrhythmic drug; in cardiac arrest it is used for shock-refractory VF or pulseless VT.
A drug once used in cardiac arrest; no longer part of the AHA adult cardiac arrest algorithm.
A thin tube in the ureter with one coil in the kidney pelvis and one in the bladder, holding the ureter open.
Mineral crust building up on a stent or catheter, which can block it.
Two stomas side by side: the proximal one passes stool, the distal one only mucus.
A tiny pacemaker placed inside a heart chamber through the femoral vein, with no leads.
Being open and flowing freely (e.g. an IV that flushes easily with no swelling).
Two drugs or fluids that react when mixed (cloudiness, crystals, color change). Stop, and don't flush it into the patient.
A patient's ability to understand information and make a decision. Without it, a legal representative gives consent.
An inflatable wrist band that presses on the radial artery puncture to stop bleeding after radial access.
An MRI scanner with a larger opening (or an open design) that helps claustrophobic or larger patients.
How much tracer a tissue takes in. In PET, the quiet waiting time after injection while FDG is absorbed.
How easily seizures are triggered. Some drugs lower it, which matters before myelography.
An ARRT credential earned after a primary one (e.g. CT, MR, mammography, VI, CI).
X-ray imaging of the breast, using compression. Screening is for no symptoms; diagnostic is for a symptom or an abnormal screen.
The eardrum. A tympanic thermometer reads its infrared heat, which tracks core temperature.
Fire evacuation that moves people sideways first, through a fire door to a safe area on the same floor, before using stairs.
